conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions about the past week, and it helps us spot anything from normal “baby blues” to signs of depression or anxiety that deserve extra care. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll go at your pace; there are no right or wrong answers, only your honest experience. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. I can still laugh a little if something’s genuinely hilarious, but most of the time I feel like I’m faking it. It’s like the joy is behind a pane of glass—I can see it, but I can’t quite reach it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly no… maybe once or twice the whole week when my partner made a silly joke, but even then it felt forced. I’d smile, but the laughter just doesn’t bubble up the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels flat. I still go through the motions, hoping the enjoyment will kick in, but it’s like I’m just ticking boxes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more than I’d like to admit. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m not a good enough mom.” I know logically it’s not always my fault, but the guilt still shows up almost every day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s a low hum of worry running in the background—about the baby breathing, about whether I’m holding him right, about things that haven’t even happened. Sometimes I can talk myself down, but the next wave just rolls in.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times—mostly at night when the house is quiet. My heart starts racing and I feel like something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. It passes if I get up and walk around, but in the moment it’s hard to catch my breath.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The diapers, the feedings, the dishes—individually they’re tiny, but together they pile up until I’m frozen on the couch, staring at the mess and thinking, “I can’t do this.” I still manage, but it’s like clawing my way up a hill that keeps getting steeper.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah. A couple of nights this week I couldn’t fall asleep even though the baby was out. My mind just kept circling—what if he stops breathing, what if I mess something up tomorrow—until I was staring at the ceiling for hours. When I do sleep, I wake up with a jolt, heart pounding, and then it’s hard to drift off again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s not tears-all-day awful, but there’s this heavy sadness that sits on my chest from the moment I open my eyes. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like I could cry for no real reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’d say twice this week. Yesterday I put the baby in the crib, shut the door, and just sobbed in the hallway. Nothing huge happened—he wouldn’t nap and I felt like I’d failed him. The tears come fast and then leave me exhausted.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s crossed my mind. Not a plan or anything—I’d never leave my baby—but when I’m really overwhelmed I get this quick flash of “what if I just weren’t here.” It scares me, and I push it away, but it’s popped up once or twice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today’s date]  
Source: Self-report via EPDS-10 interview  

A. Positive Screening Indicators  
- Depressed mood: daily sadness, frequent tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Anhedonia: marked loss of interest/enjoyment in previously pleasant activities (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding parenting competence (Q3)  
- Persistent, unprovoked anxiety and nocturnal panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed by routine tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia: difficulty initiating and returning to sleep despite infant resting (Q7)  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan/intent): “what if I just weren’t here,” twice this week (Q10)  

B. Pattern Summary  
Responses cluster in domains consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety. Functional impact described as “clawing my way up a hill,” indicating significant distress and impaired coping.  

C. Risk Considerations  
- Safety: presence of any self-harm ideation, even if passive → requires immediate formal risk assessment.  
- Protective factors endorsed: strong attachment to infant, partner support noted, denies intent.  
- No psychotic features elicited.  

D. Screening Conclusion  
Findings exceed threshold for routine depression/anxiety surveillance; recommend expedited clinical evaluation (diagnostic interview, standardized rating scales, safety plan) and consideration of perinatal mental health specialty referral.
